extracted.intended_audience: learned natural philosophers, chymists, and students of natural philosophy (early-modern scientific audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing chymical/elemental hypotheses and the quality of the arguments and experiments offered in natural philosophy; emphasizes when experiments are persuasive, explanatory scope, consistency, and methodological caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize experiments over speculative reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the experiments of opponents rather than their speculative reasons; value empirical operations and observations above mere speculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carneades states he would 'Examine only the Experiments of my Adversaries, not their Speculative Reasons.' The text repeatedly praises the usefulness of chymists' experiments but criticises their speculative writings: 'their Furnaces, afford as well smoke as light.' Anti-pattern: accepting speculative theory without weighing experimental evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judging nature of bodies by a single shared quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conclude bodies are of the same nature merely because they share one general quality (e.g., fluidity, dryness, volatility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that resemblances in one quality can mask large disparities in others, so identification by a single shared trait is a 'gross Way of judging.' Example: different dry substances (calxes of gold, vitriol, Venetian talc, ashes) differ despite being 'dry.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Require demonstrative, not merely specious, experimental proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments cited to support a doctrine must be demonstrative and convincing, not merely specious or accomodatable to multiple hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that 'the Vulgar Experiments ... wont to be Alledg'd by Chymists ... are not so demonstrative as to reduce a wary Person to acquiesce.' Anti-pattern: treating easily reinterpretable experiments as definitive proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory scope: theory must account for wide range of phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory hypothesis should explain not only a narrow set of laboratory cases but also wider natural phenomena (e.g., celestial bodies, biological generation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carneades criticises the Tria Prima for failing to account for the Sun, fixed stars, formation of chicks in eggs, and other large-scale or biological phenomena. Criterion: test a theory's reach beyond the limited domain where it was devised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and quantification where required
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory should state proportions, quantities, or mechanisms when needed to produce natural objects or phenomena (e.g., 'how much Salt, how much Sulphur, and how much Mercury must be taken').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author demands concrete proportions and an account of what agent/mixture constructs complex structures; anti-pattern: vague appeals to 'some subtle part' doing the work without specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overgeneralizing from limited or local experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not generalize a new 'philosophy' from experiments on a limited class of compound bodies; beware claiming a universal system from narrow observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chymists were criticised for proclaiming a New Philosophy based on resolution of some compound bodies while ignoring the vast diversity of the universe. Example: successful decompositions on terrestrial crust do not justify sweeping cosmological claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for internal consistency and non-contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses and inferences must be consistent; a theorist should not assign contradictory accounts to the same phenomena or substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author points out an author who first analyzes green wood's 'sweat' as water, smoke as air, shining matter as fire, and ashes as earth, but later finds the four elements in each of those parts—this self-contradiction exposes incompetency of the analysis. Anti-pattern: shifting categorizations to fit conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of arguments amenable to multiple hypotheses (non-discriminating evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an argument or experimental result can be accommodated by multiple competing hypotheses, it is not discriminating evidence for any single one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carneades notes that a way of arguing may be 'speciously accommodated to differing Hypotheses' (e.g., both Tria Prima and Tria Prima critics can reinterpret results). Anti-pattern: treating such ambivalent evidence as decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer a unique native subject from shared qualities without proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume that because many bodies share a quality, that quality must be seated in a single common material principle or subject without demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting and critiquing Sennertus' syllogism, Carneades calls the major premise 'precarious'—showing shared qualities (colours, odors, flavours) do not prove a single underlying principle. Anti-pattern: jump from correlation to single-cause attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure mapping of properties to principles is coherent and non-overlapping
rubrics_metrics.description: A good doctrine should not ascribe the same wide-ranging qualities to multiple different principles such that the distinctions collapse (e.g., volatility or fluidity assigned to all principles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text observes chymists ascribing tastes and coagulation to salt, odour and inflammability to sulphur, colours to mercury, yet also admitting volatility in all three—this undermines the distinctness of principles. Anti-pattern: indistinct property assignments that make principles meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret experimental products carefully to avoid misclassification
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental exhalations, condensates, or 'vapours' should be analysed cautiously; what appears as 'air' or 'vapour' may be aggregates of liquid droplets or other artefacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When vapour caught in glasses condenses to drops, it is misclassified as air; likewise, apparent flame-parts may be adventitious heat rather than elemental fire. Anti-pattern: taking superficial appearances as proof of elemental composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize methodological limits and artefacts of decomposition techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods (e.g., resolution by fire) may create new compounds or artefacts and so cannot be assumed to reveal true elementary constituents of a body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that substances separable by fire are 'not for the most part pure and Elementary bodies, but new kinds of mixts.' Thus decomposition by heat can be misleading. Anti-pattern: assuming method yields unaltered primitives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false dichotomies; do not infer truth of one hypothesis from falsity of another
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the fallacy that only two positions exist; the falsity of one hypothesis does not automatically validate another absent positive evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns disputants often frame two-opinion choices; many questions admit multiple competing hypotheses. Anti-pattern: concluding the Tria Prima is true simply because the four-element theory is flawed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand explanatory power for obvious, familiar phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory theory should explain even simple, familiar phenomena (fluidity, firmness, colours, nutrition, gravity) and not only obscure or rare cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carneades stresses that inability to account for 'obvious and more familiar Phænomena' undermines a theory. Example: a theory that cannot explain why gold is heavier than quicksilver in certain contexts is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious when using terminological/conceptual conflations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conflate different concepts (e.g., fluidity vs humidity) in argumentation; precise distinction of terms matters to sound reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carneades reproaches Guntherus for confounding fluidity with humidity. Anti-pattern: sloppy use of language that masks conceptual errors and yields invalid inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require ocular/replicable demonstration when claiming elemental presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that elements are present in a substance should be supported by clear, replicable, ocular demonstration rather than inference alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critiqued author professes to give 'an occular Demonstration' of elements from burning wood; Carneades demands such demonstrations be robust and not self-contradictory. Anti-pattern: asserting elemental presence without reproducible demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check causal explanations for agents and mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: When attributing formation or properties to mixtures of principles, specify what agent or process arranges those ingredients into the observed structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text questions what 'Architectonick Spirit' or agent contrives mixtures into bones, veins, feathers, etc., if only three principles are admitted. Anti-pattern: postulating an unexplained 'director' that merely relieves the theory of mechanistic detail.
